passage:
In temperate forests a tree lays down one layer of wood each growing season, and the width of that layer records the conditions under which it formed. Width by itself, however, tells an observer very little. A ring may be narrow because the summer was dry, because a neighbour's canopy closed over the crown, or simply because the tree was old. Dendrochronology becomes a dating method only when the variation shared by many trees can be separated from the variation peculiar to one.

That separation is possible where a single factor limits growth across a whole stand. On a shallow, well-drained slope the limit is water; near the upper treeline it is summer warmth. Trees growing under such a constraint respond together: a drought year leaves a narrow ring in every trunk on the site, and a favourable year a wide one. What emerges is not a smooth trend but a jagged, unrepeated pattern of wide and narrow rings, and it is the pattern, rather than any single measurement, that a dendrochronologist matches.

Matching proceeds backwards. A core taken from a living tree yields a sequence whose outermost ring was formed in the season of coring, so every ring inward can be assigned a calendar year without further argument. Timber from a barn built two centuries earlier will overlap that sequence at its older end; where the two patterns coincide, the barn's rings acquire dates as well, and the chronology is carried further back. Repeated with progressively older material, first beams, then bog oaks, then logs buried in river gravels, the procedure has extended some regional chronologies beyond nine thousand years.

A sequence that has been measured but not yet joined to this framework is called a floating chronology. Its internal spacing is known exactly; what it lacks is a fixed point. A floating chronology from a prehistoric settlement may establish, with complete confidence, that one house was built forty-one years after another, while leaving open the century in which either was built.
prompt: [Academic — Archaeology] What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Ring widths can date wood because trees on a limiting site share a pattern that can be carried from one piece of timber to the next.
The width of a single ring is a dependable record of one year's rainfall once the age of the tree has been taken into account.
The chronologies that reach back thousands of years were assembled from bog oaks and buried logs rather than from trees now living.
Dendrochronologists work backwards through time because recent timber is easier to obtain than prehistoric timber.
correct_answer: Ring widths can date wood because trees on a limiting site share a pattern that can be carried from one piece of timber to the next.
explanation: The passage first isolates the problem, that a ring may be narrow for reasons "peculiar to one" tree, then solves it with a stand in which one factor limits growth, then walks the shared pattern back through older wood; that is the statement about a pattern "carried from one piece of timber to the next." The rainfall statement makes a single ring dependable, which the first paragraph denies. The bog oaks and buried logs are one step in the third paragraph's procedure, not the passage's point. And no paragraph says recent timber is easier to obtain; the reason matching runs backwards is that only a living tree's outermost ring has a known date.

correct_answer: To show how wood whose dates are already fixed can pass those dates to older wood that overlaps it.

passage:
Not every tree keeps a usable record. Where water is abundant and the season long, no single factor governs growth, and the tree lays down rings of nearly uniform width year after year. Such a series is called complacent. It will fit almost any sequence offered to it, and for that reason it dates nothing; the sites that yield the best chronologies are the harsh ones, where trees grow badly and unevenly.

Two counting errors trouble even a sensitive series. In a year of extreme stress a tree may add no measurable wood around part of its trunk, so that a core drilled through that sector passes directly from one year to the next; the ring is absent rather than thin. The opposite error arises when a midsummer drought is broken by late rain. The tree produces a band of small, dense cells and then resumes growing, and that band closely resembles the boundary between two seasons. Neither error announces itself on a single core. Cross-dating exposes both, because a core with one ring missing falls out of register with its neighbours by precisely one year, and the mismatch persists through every earlier ring.

A further difficulty concerns what a date refers to. Wood near the centre of a trunk is dead heartwood; only the outer sapwood rings are living tissue at the moment of felling. A carpenter squaring a beam commonly cuts the sapwood away, and decay removes much of what the axe leaves. When the outermost surviving ring on a beam is heartwood, the figure recovered is not the felling date but a limit: the tree came down in that year or in some later year, and how much later depends on how many sapwood rings are gone. Regional tables give an expected range for the missing rings, but the correction is statistical rather than exact.

Even a secure felling date dates the tree. Beams were salvaged from older structures and put up again, and a hall whose timbers came down in 1391 may have been raised a generation afterwards out of a demolished predecessor.

A match that is always available is no evidence, which is the option about fitting almost any sequence. The rings are called uniform, not indistinct. The counting errors and the false ring belong to the second paragraph and are presented as hazards of a sensitive series, not as the defect of a complacent one.
